Welcome to day three of health insurance subrogation training. Today is practical. We walk through how a health insurance subrogation claim is set up and worked on a real file, from intake to the final lien. Much of it is shown in FileVine, so expect screenshots, sample letters and ledgers. Your own firm's system may look different, but the steps and the reasons behind them stay the same.

Here is our road map for today. First, the process work flow, which is the order of steps on a health insurance subrogation file. Second, the CMS, meaning the case management system, where we record the health insurance and subrogation details. Third, things to remember, the practical points that keep a lien accurate and a closing on time. Keep these three headings in mind as we move through the slides.

This is the health insurance subro work flow from start to finish, in two parts. It begins at intake. Then we open the third-party or first-party claim, prepare the client information, send the letter of representation and HIPAA, and put the health insurance company on notice. Notice that all of this happens early, long before there is any lien amount to review. Ask yourself: which of these steps depends on what the client told us at intake? Continuing the flow, we set up the health insurance subro claim, generate the subrogation letter, send it to the subrogation company, and then confirm receipt and follow up after sixty days. Keep in mind that the step seven slides later say to verify receipt within fifteen to thirty days. Treat the early call as confirming the letter arrived, and the later follow-up as chasing the lien itself.

This is the subrogation checklist you will use on intake. It asks whether the client has health insurance, whether an uninsured client should apply for Medicaid, whether the client wants to use their health insurance, whether we have copies of the card, and whether a letter of representation went out to start subrogation. Then it lists where treatment happened: ambulance, hospital, urgent care with its name, and any other treatment on health insurance.

The second half of the checklist follows the file forward. Did we receive a notice of lien, and if not, what is missing? Did we send a letter to bill health insurance, and did the missing providers send their bills? Is the client done treating, has the case settled, and has the final subrogation lien been received? Read the note on the form about requesting the final lien, and the Medicare exception.

Here we cover the notice of lien. It is correspondence from the health insurance provider to the law firm saying it may have paid claims tied to the accident and expects reimbursement when the case concludes. Treat it as an official claim against the recovery. Log it, save it to the file, and update your lien tracking. A notice is not yet the final amount; it tells us the plan has an interest.

This slide explains what the notice means for us. It represents a lien on the settlement. The health insurance subrogation company is waiting for the law firm to reimburse the health insurance provider once the case is resolved. In other words, the money comes out of the settlement through our office, so we are responsible for making sure that lien is handled before the client is paid.

Here is a sample notice of lien from Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield. Look at the header with the member, the date of loss and the plan's file number. The letter says the plan is subrogated to the member's rights of recovery and asks us to consult them before resolving the claim. The highlighted line tells us to treat this letter as notice of the plan's subrogation rights.

Now we move to the step by step guide for setting up a health insurance subrogation claim. Each step builds on the one before, from checking intake to requesting the final lien. The screenshots come from FileVine, so the buttons in your system may differ, but the order of the work is what matters.

Step one is to check intake and look for the motor vehicle accident questionnaire. In FileVine it sits in the Intake section, as the screenshot shows. The questionnaire tells us what the client reported about the accident and their treatment, which is where our health insurance work starts. Remember the note: this is presented in FileVine and may vary depending on the firm.

Step two is confirming whether the client was transported to the hospital. Ask three questions. Was the client taken to a hospital, and which one? Was the client transported by EMS, and which company? Were x-rays or CT scans taken? Each answer points to a provider whose bills may have gone to health insurance, so each one may end up on the lien.

Step three is obtaining the health insurance information and ID. Call the member services number on the back of the client's card. Ask how to send letters of representation and the HIPAA authorization, and confirm whether they handle subrogation themselves. Then write down the particulars they give you. Having a copy of the card on file makes this call much quicker. One important caution on that call. Do not provide any information about the defendant's insurance, the claim number or other pertinent details. Member services only needs what it takes to identify our client and set up the subrogation file. Share only what is needed, and let the attorney decide what else, if anything, goes to the plan.

Step four is setting up the health subrogation information in your case management system. In FileVine, open the Insurance-Health section shown here. This is where the insured party, the claims adjuster and the insurance company are recorded. Getting this right now saves everyone time later, because every letter we generate pulls from these fields.

This screen shows the fields to complete in the health insurance record. The insurance type, the insured party, the name of the client exactly as it appears on the card, the insurance company, the member ID number and the group number are all marked in red. Check each against the card itself. A wrong member ID can stall the subrogation set-up for weeks.

Last part of step four. Mark Subro as yes and fill in the subrogation company. In this example it is The Rawlings Group. The callout says to update the subrogation contact card, so the company's details are ready when you generate letters. If the plan uses an outside vendor, that vendor is who we correspond with.

Step five is generating the letter of subrogation. In FileVine, go to Insurance-Health, and under Health Insurance Subrogation you will see the Regenerate button, highlighted here. Below it is the abundance of caution letter, which we will meet again later. Generating from the system keeps the client and insurance details consistent with what you entered in step four.

This screenshot shows the two clicks. Click Generate or Regenerate to create the letter, then use the arrow beside the file name to download it, or preview it first. Always open the downloaded letter and read it before sending. A generated letter is only as accurate as the fields behind it.

Next we edit the subrogation letter of representation before it goes out with a signed HIPAA form. Here is a sample. The highlights show what to check: the sending method at the top, the greeting, and the enclosure line listing the HIPAA. Read the body too, so the client details and dates match the file.

Pay attention to how the letter will be sent: by fax, first-class mail, email, or a mix. Then state that method at the top of the letter, as the sample does. That line becomes our record of how and where we sent the request, which matters if the company later says it never received it.

Now the HIPAA form. In FileVine it is saved in the Intake section, as shown. Download the HIPAA form and edit it for this request. The signed authorization is what allows the health insurer to share the client's information with us, so it has to go out with the letter.

Here is the HIPAA authorization itself. The callout says to put the name of the provider, which here means the health insurance company we are sending it to. Check the client's name, date of birth and other details against the file before attaching it.

Once the HIPAA is downloaded, attach it to the letter. In Nitro, use the insert or combine function; the screenshot shows Edit, then Insert, then Insert from file. The result is one document: the letter followed by the signed HIPAA. Sending them together means the company has everything it needs in a single request.

Step six is sending the letter with the health insurance card. It may go by fax, email or regular mail. This screenshot shows a fax sent through email: add 1 at the beginning of the fax number and the fax service address, and use the subject line format client's name, insurance provider, type of letter. A clear subject line makes the request easy to find later.

Step seven is confirming receipt. Verify with the subrogation company within fifteen to thirty days that our letter was received and that a case has been set up on their side. The typical turnaround for the initial lien is thirty days. So if you call at day twenty and they have no record, you have time to resend before the delay builds.

Some companies ask for first-party or third-party insurance information. Instead, we can provide a lien protection letter, which guarantees that the lien will be settled when the case resolves. It is a commitment that we will protect the lien out of the settlement, so only send it when it is appropriate and approved on the file.

Here is a sample lien protection letter. It identifies the insured, member ID, client, date of birth and date of loss. It explains why we will not share the third-party insurance information, citing NRPC 1.15(d) and the collateral source rule, and promises to protect the plan's interest and satisfy the lien when the case ends. This letter is a promise from the firm, so use the approved template.

Step eight is reviewing the subrogation lien. Save it in the health insurance tab of your case management system and update the lien amount. Then check that the claims include the hospital, ER physician, radiology, ambulance and any other providers who billed health insurance. Make sure the amount matches the bills recorded under the medications tab. Gaps here usually mean a bill is missing somewhere.

If providers have the health insurance information and billed it correctly, give the claims time to process and request the lien again after a month. If a bill shows a health insurance payment but that claim is not on the lien, send an abundance letter. An incomplete lien now can turn into a surprise later, after funds have gone out.

Here is a sample abundance letter. It goes to the subrogation company, refers to their earlier letter, and lists the provider and amount that was paid but left off the lien. The highlighted fields are the parts you complete. Send it with the medical bill that shows the health insurance payment, so the company can see exactly what to add.

The other side of step eight is removing claims that do not belong. If unrelated claims are on the lien, send a request for removal. For example, a routine visit for an ongoing condition that has nothing to do with the accident should not be repaid out of the injury settlement. Be specific, so the request is easy to act on.

This is a sample subrogation removal request letter. Look at how it lists each claim to be removed, line by line, with the items highlighted. Listing the items this precisely makes the request easy for the subrogation company to process, and gives us a clear record of what we disputed.

If providers do not have the health insurance information, their claims will not be processed, so they will not appear on the lien. Ideally the patient gives that information at the time of service. If the patient did not, we can send the health insurance information to the provider ourselves. That gets the bill processed through insurance instead of sitting unpaid.

Step nine is requesting the final lien. The goal is simple: obtain a final subrogation letter. Until we have it, any lien amount on the file is only an estimate. The final letter is the figure the closing statement and the disbursement will rely on.

When the case moves to settlement, request the final lien. Some companies require settlement information before they send it, so have those details ready. Then update the disbursement sheet with the final number so the closing statement is accurate. A common mistake is disbursing using an old interim figure instead of the final lien.

This optional letter asks a provider to bill the client's health insurance. Here is a sample. It sets out the client, date of birth and date of loss, then the health insurance name, member ID, address and phone, and asks the provider to bill the plan. It goes out with the HIPAA and a copy of the health insurance card.

Sometimes ER physicians prefer to be paid through the settlement rather than through insurance. If that happens, after sending the billing letter with the HIPAA release and insurance card, contact the ER physician and ask them to return the bills to the hospital so the hospital can bill the insurance. The slide cites a New York Times article for background.

After the bills have been submitted, call the subrogation department and request the updated subrogation lien ledger. Plan for the wait: updated liens take anywhere from two weeks to thirty to sixty days. Put a follow-up date on the file so the request does not get lost while the case moves toward settlement.

A final subrogation lien letter is the formal communication from the insurer or provider asking for reimbursement of what it paid on behalf of the insured or injured party. Two things make it important: it confirms the final amount of the lien, and it outlines the subrogation claim. This is the document the disbursement is built on.

Here is a sample of our side of that exchange: a letter from the firm asking for the final lien. It says the case is in final negotiations with the third-party insurer and requests a final subrogation lien. The highlighted parts, such as the sending method and client details, are what you complete for each file.

Before the next slide, a definition. A cost-benefit analysis is a systematic way to weigh the benefits of a decision against its costs, financial and non-financial. It helps decide whether an action is worth taking. We use this thinking when deciding whether a disputed bill on a lien is worth the time it takes to remove.

This slide is about judgment. Review the lien again to make sure all relevant bills are on it, and request removal of irrelevant ones. But weigh the cost-benefit. If a disputed charge is small and removing it would take hours of calls and letters, it may not be worth the fight. Pick your battles.

Here is a sample final lien letter from Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield. Find the final lien amount, the instructions for where and how to send payment, and the plan's file number to include with the check. These are the details that go onto the disbursement sheet and the payment itself.

This is the claim summary that comes with a final lien. It lists each service date, provider, diagnosis codes, the amount billed and the amount paid, then any amount previously recovered and the total. Below it are the codes with their descriptions. Use this page to check that each claim relates to the accident before accepting the final figure.

Once the final ledger is in, you can request a reduction of the lien. There are three possible outcomes. The reduction may be approved, and you pay the reduced amount. It may be rejected. Or the company may make a counteroffer, proposing a different amount or asking for settlement information, which you can choose to provide or accept. Get any agreed reduction in writing.

Two more samples, and both answer a reduction request. On the left, a UnitedHealthcare fax says a thirty-five percent reduction was denied, but the lien was reduced by thirty percent as a show of good faith. On the right, the Culinary Health Fund reviews the settlement figures and declines to recommend a reduction. Whatever the layout, find the final amount, the payee and the reference number.

This is a subrogation lien ledger. The service dates are boxed in red because that is the first thing to check. Each line shows the claim number, provider, diagnosis codes, amount billed and amount paid. At the bottom is the total and the final lien payment instruction. Read every line before you accept the total.

When reading the ledger, check that the dates and services are linked to the incident. Compare against your records to see whether all bills are accounted for. Decide whether to request bills and records, which usually depends on whether you need them for the demand. If you do not recognize a provider, research it online to see whether it connects to the collision.

Check the lien for any bills that are absent, and ask for any bills you need to confirm the figures are accurate. But there are situations where it is best not to request the bills and records, especially when the policy limits have been exceeded and the funds need to be interpleaded. Check with the attorney before deciding.

That brings us to the end of day three. We covered the health insurance subrogation work flow from intake through the final lien and the lien ledger. Take a few minutes to review the checklist and the sample letters, and bring any questions about your own files to the next session.
